innate obesity is revealed by selection markers and is associated with a significant imprint of hypothalamic genes controlling energy expenditure.

the identification of the genes and gene networks that underlie the innate predisposition to develop obesity and the identification of novel therapeutic targets to treat this global epidemic.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are significant differences in the regulation of energy expenditure between sheep and rodents.
the hypothalamus is the key regulator of energy balance and that the hypothalamo-pituitary axis, in particular, is a major determinant of the susceptibility to become obese.
the propensity to become overweight or obese in response to an energy-rich environment is a function of innate differences in the hypothalamus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are innate differences in the hypothalamus of animals selected for obesity and/or cortisol responsiveness that lead to altered energy expenditure and propensity to become obese.
the propensity of animals to become obese can be determined, at least in large part, by the innate differences in hypothalamic gene expression that are associated with altered energy expenditure.
obesity is a complex trait, with a polygenic basis and the hypothalamus plays an integral role in determining innate predispositions to weight gain and obesity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the hypothalamus plays an important role in innate predisposition to weight gain and obesity, and that the hypothalamic circuitry controlling energy expenditure is the primary determinant of this phenotype.
the hypothalamic melanocortin system is the primary target for the selection of lean sheep and the main target for the selection for high and low cortisol responsiveness in sheep and mice.
